title: Weak reasoning and logical fallacies
blurb: Recognize the fourteen common fallacies and tell the look-alikes apart: straw man vs ad hominem, post hoc vs slippery slope.
question: A council member says, 'My opponent wants a bike lane on Main Street, so she obviously wants to ban cars downtown.' A TEAS item asks which fallacy this is. Is it ad hominem or straw man, and how can you tell?

teach.h: Fallacies: reasoning that only looks strong
teach.body: Formally, a logical fallacy is an error in reasoning: the support offered does not actually prove the conclusion, even though it may sound convincing. In plain English: a fallacy is a trick or a slip that makes an argument seem better than it is. The TEAS asks you to recognize common fallacies by name and to see why the reasoning fails, whether or not you agree with the conclusion.

children.label: Dodge the argument
children.sub: Ad hominem, straw man, red herring

teach.h: Naming a fallacy in four moves
items: Find the conclusion the speaker wants you to accept.
Find what is offered as support.
Ask what is wrong with the link: wrong target (the person)? Wrong version of the other view? Weak cause? Too few cases? Pressure instead of proof? Too few choices? Conclusion assumed?
Match the flaw to the name, then check the look-alike before you commit.

rows.label: Attacks
values: A distorted version of the view

rows.label: Sounds like
values: She can't drive, so ignore her
He wants lanes, so he hates cars

rows.label: Ask
values: Is this about who they are?
Is this what they really said?

rows.label: Logic
values: B after A, so A caused B

rows.label: Signal
values: Places with more X have more Y

teach.caption: Post hoc looks backward at a sequence; slippery slope looks forward to a predicted chain.

teach.text: The most-tested mix-ups: straw man vs ad hominem (twisting the view vs insulting the person) and post hoc vs slippery slope (a past sequence vs a predicted chain). Also, a fallacy is about the reasoning: a conclusion you agree with can still be supported by a fallacy.

teach.body: Carlos Mendoza, applying to a paramedic program, reads: 'My opponent wants a bike lane on Main Street, so she obviously wants to ban cars downtown.' He asks: is the speaker attacking her as a person? No, nothing about her character. Is the speaker restating her view accurately? No: a bike lane is not a car ban. The speaker has replaced her real position with an extreme one that is easier to knock down. Carlos picks straw man.

teach.h: Why fallacies matter on the TEAS
teach.body: Fallacy items test whether you judge support rather than conclusions. A writer can be right about bike lanes and still argue with a straw man. When an item asks why an argument is weak, the answer names the broken link (too few cases, a cause assumed from timing, an expert from the wrong field), not a reason you happen to disagree with the claim.

items: A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning, not a false conclusion.
Ad hominem attacks the person; straw man distorts the position.
Post hoc: after, so because of. Slippery slope: one step leads to disaster.
Hasty generalization and anecdotes draw big claims from too little evidence.
Bandwagon, false authority, emotion and tradition apply pressure instead of proof.
False dilemma offers two choices; circular reasoning assumes its conclusion.

summary: You can now recognize the common logical fallacies by name and explain why each one fails to support its conclusion. You can also separate the look-alikes, especially straw man from ad hominem and post hoc from slippery slope.

A.q:
At a school board meeting, a parent says: 'Mr. Daniels wants to cut the field trip budget, but he doesn't even have children, so why should we listen to anything he says about schools?'

Which fallacy does the parent commit?
A.why: The parent dismisses Mr. Daniels' proposal by pointing to a personal fact about him rather than addressing the budget argument. That is an attack on the person.

whyNot.1: The parent does not misstate Mr. Daniels' proposal; he really does want to cut the budget.
whyNot.2: The parent stays on the subject of Mr. Daniels and his proposal rather than switching topics.
whyNot.3: No broad conclusion is drawn from a few examples.

A.q:
A flyer reads: 'Either the city raises property taxes this year, or our public libraries will have to close for good. There is no other way.'

Which fallacy does the flyer contain?
A.why: The flyer presents only two options (raise taxes or close libraries) when others likely exist, such as cutting hours, seeking grants or moving money from other programs.

whyNot.0: There is no chain of steps leading to an extreme outcome; it is a single either/or choice.
whyNot.1: The conclusion is not assumed in the premise.
whyNot.3: The flyer does not appeal to what most people believe or do.

A.q:
An ad says: 'Over two million Americans start their day with VitaBoost shakes. Isn't it time you joined them?'

Which fallacy does the ad rely on?
A.why: The ad argues that the shake is worth buying because many people use it. Popularity is offered in place of evidence that the product works.

whyNot.0: The ad points to how many people use the shake, not to how long it has been used.
whyNot.1: No expert or celebrity is cited.
whyNot.2: The ad makes no claim that one event caused another because of their order.

B.q:
A senator says: 'My colleague supports a modest increase in funding for school nurses. Apparently she thinks we should hand unlimited money to schools with no oversight at all.'

Which fallacy does the senator commit?
B.why: The senator replaces the colleague's real position (a modest increase) with an extreme version (unlimited money, no oversight) that is easier to attack.

whyNot.0: The senator attacks a distorted version of the policy, not the colleague's character.
whyNot.2: No choice is reduced to two options.
whyNot.3: The statement distorts a position; it does not use emotion as its support.

B.q:
A blogger writes: 'I started drinking green tea in March, and in April my seasonal allergies cleared up. Green tea cured my allergies.'

Which fallacy does the blogger commit?
B.why: The blogger assumes that because the allergies improved after starting tea, the tea caused the improvement. Seasonal allergies often change with the season itself.

whyNot.0: There is no predicted chain of future events.
whyNot.2: The blogger stays on the topic of the allergies.
whyNot.3: The blogger is not generalizing about a group; the error is assuming cause from timing.

B.q:
A student argues: 'Our school's honor code is fair because it treats every student justly.'

Which fallacy does the student commit?
B.why: 'Fair' and 'treats every student justly' mean the same thing, so the reason simply restates the conclusion. The claim is assumed rather than proven.

whyNot.1: The student does not argue that the code is right because it is old or customary.

C.q:
A report notes: 'Cities with more coffee shops per person also have higher average incomes. To raise incomes, cities should encourage more coffee shops to open.'

Which fallacy does the report commit?
C.why: Coffee shops and income rise together, but that link does not show shops cause higher income; wealthier areas may simply attract more shops.

whyNot.0: No expert or celebrity is cited.
whyNot.1: There is no predicted chain of events leading to an extreme outcome.
whyNot.2: The report does not appeal to custom or past practice.

C.q:
During a debate on hospital staffing, a board member is asked whether nurses on the night shift have enough support. She replies: 'What I'd really like to talk about is the beautiful new lobby we opened last month.'

Which fallacy is this?
C.why: The board member shifts attention to an unrelated topic (the lobby) to avoid the staffing question. That is a red herring.

whyNot.0: She does not attack the person who asked.
whyNot.1: She does not appeal to what most people think or do.

C.q:
A columnist writes: 'I asked five friends whether our county's new recycling rules are working, and four said no. Clearly, most county residents think the rules have failed.'

Which statement best explains why the argument is weak?
options: It attacks the people who wrote the recycling rules.
It draws a broad conclusion from a small, unrepresentative group.
It assumes the rules failed because they came after a bad year.
It claims recycling rules will lead to more extreme regulations.
C.why: Five friends are too few, and too similar to the writer, to represent a whole county. That is a hasty generalization.

whyNot.0: The columnist says nothing about the people who wrote the rules.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the argument relies on timing or sequence.
whyNot.3: The columnist predicts no chain of further regulations.

reteach.title: Think of a referee calling fouls
reteach.question: A referee does not care which team wins; she only calls illegal moves. How is spotting a fallacy like calling a foul?

blocks.h: Call the move, not the score
blocks.body: A goal scored with a handball does not count, even if the team deserved to win. In the same way, a conclusion supported by a fallacy is not proven, even if it happens to be true. Your job is to call the illegal move: tripping the player instead of playing the ball (ad hominem), arguing with a cardboard cutout of the opponent (straw man), or kicking the ball out of the stadium to stop play (red herring).

blocks.text: Do not call a foul just because you dislike the team. On the TEAS, judge the reasoning, not whether you agree with the claim.

explain.body: Ad hominem attacks the person. Straw man attacks a distorted version of the person's view. Red herring changes the subject. In each case the real argument is never answered.

test.q:
A neighbor says: 'Dana wants the town to trim trees near power lines. So she wants to clear-cut every tree in town!'

Which fallacy is this?
test.why: Trimming trees near power lines is exaggerated into clear-cutting every tree, a distorted version of Dana's view that is easy to attack.

whyNot.1: Nothing is said about Dana's character or personal life.
whyNot.2: The speaker stays on the subject of trees.
whyNot.3: The conclusion is not assumed in the premise.

explain.body: Post hoc assumes that because B came after A, A caused B. Correlation as causation assumes that because two things go together, one causes the other. Slippery slope predicts that one step will lead, step by step, to an extreme result without evidence.

test.q:
A resident warns: 'If we let one food truck park downtown, soon there will be dozens, the restaurants will all close, and downtown will become a ghost town.'

Which fallacy is this?
test.why: The resident predicts that one small step will set off a chain ending in an extreme outcome, without evidence for each link.

whyNot.0: Post hoc looks back at events that already happened; this predicts future ones.
whyNot.1: The resident does not offer just two options.
whyNot.3: No appeal is made to what most people do or believe.

explain.body: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases. Anecdotal evidence treats one personal story as proof. Both mistake a sample that is too small for a pattern.

test.q:
Someone argues: 'My uncle never wore a seat belt and drove for fifty years without a scratch, so seat belts aren't necessary.'

Which fallacy is this?
test.why: One person's experience is treated as proof about seat belts in general. That is anecdotal evidence.

whyNot.0: The uncle is not presented as an expert.
whyNot.1: The argument is not that seat belts are wrong because things have always been done another way.
whyNot.2: The speaker stays on the topic of seat belts.

explain.body: Bandwagon: many people do it. False authority: a celebrity or an expert in another field says so. Appeal to emotion or fear: feelings replace evidence. Appeal to tradition: it has always been done this way.

test.q:
A commercial shows a famous pop singer saying, 'I trust BrightSmile toothpaste to keep my teeth healthy, and you should too.'

Which fallacy does the commercial use?
test.why: A singer is not an expert in dental health, so her endorsement is offered as proof by someone without relevant authority.

whyNot.0: The ad relies on one celebrity, not on how many people use the product.
whyNot.2: The ad does not claim the toothpaste is good because it has always been used.
whyNot.3: No broad conclusion is drawn from a small sample.
